A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex vector space with a norm $\|\cdot\|$. Then $\|\cdot\|$ is induced by an inner product on $V$ if and only if it satisfies the parallelogram law

$$\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2 \qquad (x,y\in V).$$

In that case the inner product is unique, and it is given by the real polarisation formula

$$\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2\bigr)$$

in the real case, and by the complex polarisation formula

$$\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2+i\|x+iy\|^2-i\|x-iy\|^2\bigr)$$

in the complex case with the first-variable-linear convention.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]),
with the root convention that
each inner product is linear in its first argument. Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for
the complex-linear endomorphisms of $H$ and $\mathcal L(H,K)$ for the
complex-linear maps from $H$ to $K$ ([[def-linear-map]]). A **finite Kraus
representation** of a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ is a finite family
$(K_a)_{a\in A}\subseteq\mathcal L(H,K)$ such that

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space. If $D:V\to V$ is linear
and $\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)=0$ for every linear map $A:V\to V$, then $D=0$.
Equivalently, the trace pairing $(D,A)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)$
has the property that its only first input pairing to zero with every second
input is $D=0$. This includes the zero space.

=\sum_a\operatorname{tr}_H(K_a^\dagger K_aX)=\operatorname{tr}_H(SX)$.
If $S=I_H$, this equals $\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$ for every $X$, so $\Phi$

$H=0$, where $I_H=0$.

Conversely, suppose $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of $\mathcal L(H)$.

$\operatorname{tr}_H((S-I_H)X)=0$ for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$. Apply [F4]
with $A=S-I_H$ to obtain $S-I_H=0$. Thus the normalization holds. In
particular, if $H=0$ both sides are the unique zero endomorphism and the
argument still applies.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}$ be finite-dimensional (have
finite bases by [[def-dimension]]) complex inner-product spaces
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and fix an
ordered orthonormal basis $\mathcal B=(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1})$ of

([[def-linear-map]]),
$E_{ij}x:=\langle x,e_j\rangle e_i$, using the root inner product convention

If $\dim H=0$ or $\dim K=0$, the input or output operator space is zero,
so $\Phi=0$ and the empty family is a Kraus representation. Assume both
dimensions are positive and choose an ordered orthonormal basis
$(f_\alpha)_{\alpha<m}$ of $K$ by [F3]. If $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)=0$, its
$(i,\alpha),(j,\beta)$ product-basis entry is the $(\alpha,\beta)$ entry
of $\Phi(E_{ij})$ by [L1], so every $\Phi(E_{ij})=0$. For each
$X\in\mathcal L(H)$, the finite sum $\sum_{i,j<n}x_{ij}E_{ij}$ whose
coordinate entries are those of $X$ agrees with $X$ on each $e_j$; [F4]
therefore makes it equal to $X$. Thus $\Phi=0$ and the empty family works
also in this case.

Suppose $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)\ne0$. Let
$S=J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)^{1/2}$ be its non-negative square root from [F2].
By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(v_a)_{a<nm}$ of $S$ with
eigenvalues $s_a\ge0$. Then
$J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)=S^2=\sum_{a:s_a>0}s_a^2v_av_a^\dagger$. For each
$a$ with $s_a>0$, put $w_a=s_av_a$ and write
$w_a=\sum_{i<n,\alpha<m}w_{a,i\alpha}e_i\otimes f_\alpha$. Define the
linear map $K_a:H\to K$ on the basis by
$K_ae_i=\sum_{\alpha<m}w_{a,i\alpha}f_\alpha$.

For every $i,j<n$ and $\alpha,\beta<m$, the
$(i,\alpha),(j,\beta)$ entry of [L1] is
$\sum_{a:s_a>0}w_{a,i\alpha}\overline{w_{a,j\beta}}$. The same entry of
$\sum_aK_aE_{ij}K_a^\dagger$ is
$\sum_a(K_a)_{\alpha i}\overline{(K_a)_{\beta j}}$, which is the same sum
because $(K_a)_{\alpha i}=w_{a,i\alpha}$ by construction and [F6] gives the
conjugate-transpose matrix of $K_a^\dagger$. Therefore
$\Phi(E_{ij})=\sum_aK_aE_{ij}K_a^\dagger$ for every matrix unit.

Every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$ is the finite coordinate combination
$\sum_{i,j<n}x_{ij}E_{ij}$ established in step 1.1. By linearity, step 1.3
therefore gives $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^\dagger$ for every $X$. There are at
most $nm=\dim(H)\dim(K)$ retained operators because the eigenbasis of $S$
has $nm$ elements; when $J=0$ the empty family was handled in step 1.1.
This is a finite Kraus representation by [L2].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K$ be a linear isometry. Then $V^\dagger V=I_H$. If $V$ is also
surjective, then $VV^\dagger=I_K$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and write $\mathcal L(H)$ and $\mathcal L(K)$ for their vector spaces of complex-linear endomorphisms with pointwise operations ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], [[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]]). Let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each integer $r\ge1$, put $R=\mathbb C^r$ with its standard ordered register basis ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). Write an operator $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ in its unique $r\times r$ block form $X=[X_{ij}]$ with $X_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H)$, and define $\Phi^{(r)}(X)$ to have blocks $[\Phi(X_{ij})]$ on $K\otimes R$. Lemma [[lem-qc-finite-ancilla-amplification-is-block-map]] proves that this block rule defines a linear map on the full operator space for every finite $r$. For $r=1$, the extension is $\Phi$ under the canonical unitary identifications $x\mapsto x\otimes e_0$ and $y\mapsto y\otimes e_0$ proved in that lemma.

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** if, for every finite $r\ge1$, $\Phi^{(r)}$ sends every nonnegative operator on $H\otimes R$ to a nonnegative operator on $K\otimes R$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]). The quantifier includes $r=1$; complete positivity therefore implies positivity. No Kraus, Choi, or Stinespring characterization is part of this definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}$ be finite-dimensional (have
finite bases by [[def-dimension]]) complex inner-product spaces
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and fix an
ordered orthonormal basis $\mathcal B=(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1})$ of
$H_{\mathrm{in}}$ (the register basis convention is in
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For $i,j<n$, let
$E_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})$ be the matrix unit, where
$\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})$ denotes the complex-linear endomorphisms
([[def-linear-map]]),
$E_{ij}x:=\langle x,e_j\rangle e_i$, using the root inner product convention
that the first argument is linear. Given a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})\to\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{out}})$
([[def-linear-map]]), its **Choi matrix relative to $\mathcal B$** is

$$J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j<n} E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}}\otimes H_{\mathrm{out}}),$$
where the operator tensor is the tensor map of [[def-qc-tensor-map]] and the
tensor inner product is the finite product pairing in
[[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]].

The tensor factors are ordered input first and output second. The coordinate
matrix has size $(n\,\dim H_{\mathrm{out}})\times(n\,\dim H_{\mathrm{out}})$.
The chosen input basis is part of this definition. Empty input or output
bases give the corresponding empty sum and zero-dimensional Choi operator.

If $\dim H=0$, [F3] makes the Choi sum empty. If $\dim K=0$, the
output operator space contains only the zero map, so every $\Phi(E_{ij})=0$.
In either case $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)=0$ is non-negative. Assume now both
spaces are nonzero, write $\mathcal B=(e_i)_{i<n}$, let
$R=\mathbb C^n$ have its standard orthonormal basis $(c_i)_{i<n}$ by [F5],
and set $\Omega=\sum_{i<n}e_i\otimes c_i$. Define
$Q_\Omega x=\langle x,\Omega\rangle\Omega$. The root pairing is linear in
its first argument, so $Q_\Omega$ is linear. For all $x,y$,
$\langle Q_\Omega x,y\rangle=
\langle x,\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega,y\rangle=
\langle x,Q_\Omega y\rangle$, and
$\langle Q_\Omega x,x\rangle=|\langle x,\Omega\rangle|^2\ge0$.
Thus $Q_\Omega$ is non-negative by [F1].

For $i,j<n$, let $F_{ij}:R\to R$ be the matrix unit
$F_{ij}c_k=0$ for $k\ne j$ and $F_{ij}c_j=c_i$. On the product basis
$(e_k\otimes c_l)$, the product pairing gives
$Q_\Omega(e_k\otimes c_l)=0$ if $k\ne l$, and
$Q_\Omega(e_k\otimes c_k)=\Omega$. The same action is given by
$\sum_{i,j<n}E_{ij}\otimes F_{ij}$, so
$Q_\Omega=\sum_{i,j<n}E_{ij}\otimes F_{ij}$ by [A2] and [A3]. The
$R$-blocks of $Q_\Omega$ are therefore $E_{ij}$; the actual block rule in
[A1] gives the non-negative operator
$Y=\Phi^{(n)}(Q_\Omega)=\sum_{i,j<n}\Phi(E_{ij})\otimes F_{ij}$ on
$K\otimes R$.

Choose an ordered orthonormal basis $(f_\alpha)_{\alpha<m}$ of $K$ by
[F2]. By [A2], both $(f_\alpha\otimes c_j)_{\alpha,j}$ and
$(e_j\otimes f_\alpha)_{j,\alpha}$ are orthonormal bases. Let
$W:K\otimes R\to H\otimes K$ be the linear map sending
$f_\alpha\otimes c_j$ to $e_j\otimes f_\alpha$. This bijection of
orthonormal bases is a surjective linear isometry; [F6] gives
$W^\dagger W=I$ and $WW^\dagger=I$. Applying the map and its inverse to
product basis vectors shows
$W(\Phi(E_{ij})\otimes F_{ij})W^\dagger=E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})$ for
each $i,j$. Hence $WY W^\dagger=J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ by [L1].

By [F4], $WY W^\dagger$ is self-adjoint because $Y$ is self-adjoint.
For every $z\in H\otimes K$, the adjoint identity gives
$\langle WY W^\dagger z,z\rangle=
\langle YW^\dagger z,W^\dagger z\rangle\ge0$, since $Y$ is
non-negative. Therefore $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is non-negative.

Fix $r\ge1$, put $R=\mathbb C^r$, and choose an ordered basis
$(c_k)_{k<r}$ of $R$. If $H=0$, the domain $\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ is zero
and the identity below holds for its sole operator. Otherwise choose an
ordered basis $(e_i)$ of $H$. Let $E_{ij}$ and $F_{kl}$ be the matrix units
in these bases. By [A2], $(e_i\otimes c_k)$ is a basis; the operators
$E_{ij}\otimes F_{kl}$ are its matrix units, so they span
$\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ by [F4] and [F5]. For such a product matrix unit,
its only nonzero ancilla block is block $(k,l)$, equal to $E_{ij}$. The block
rule in [A1] therefore gives
$\Phi^{(r)}(E_{ij}\otimes F_{kl})=\Phi(E_{ij})\otimes F_{kl}$. On the
other hand, [A3], [A4], and [L1] give
$\sum_a(K_a\otimes I_R)(E_{ij}\otimes F_{kl})(K_a^\dagger\otimes I_R)
=\sum_a(K_aE_{ij}K_a^\dagger)\otimes F_{kl}
=\Phi(E_{ij})\otimes F_{kl}$. By linearity the two maps agree for every
$X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$.

Let $X$ be non-negative and put $T_a=K_a\otimes I_R$. Each
$T_aXT_a^\dagger$ is self-adjoint because
$(T_aXT_a^\dagger)^\dagger=T_aX^\dagger T_a^\dagger=T_aXT_a^\dagger$ by
[F2]. For every $y$, the adjoint identity in [F2] gives
$\langle T_aXT_a^\dagger y,y\rangle=
\langle XT_a^\dagger y,T_a^\dagger y\rangle\ge0$ by [F1]. Thus each
summand and their finite sum are non-negative. If $A$ is empty, the sum is
zero and has the same property.

Since $r\ge1$ was arbitrary, [A1] and step 1.2 show that every finite
ancilla block amplification preserves non-negativity. This is precisely
complete positivity by [A1].

adjoint identity [F8], and the Kraus normalization give
$\|Vx\|^2=\sum_a\|K_ax\|^2

\sum_a\langle K_ax,y\rangle\langle u_a,u_b\rangle=
\langle K_bx,y\rangle=\langle x,K_b^\dagger y\rangle$. By uniqueness of
the adjoint, $V^\dagger(y\otimes u_b)=K_b^\dagger y$. Therefore, on each

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

Let $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}$ be finite-dimensional (have
finite bases by [[def-dimension]]) complex inner-product spaces
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and fix an
ordered orthonormal basis $\mathcal B=(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1})$ of
$H_{\mathrm{in}}$ (the register basis convention is in
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For $i,j<n$, let
$E_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})$ be the matrix unit, where
$\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})$ denotes the complex-linear endomorphisms
([[def-linear-map]]),
$E_{ij}x:=\langle x,e_j\rangle e_i$, using the root inner product convention
that the first argument is linear. Given a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})\to\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{out}})$
([[def-linear-map]]), its **Choi matrix relative to $\mathcal B$** is

$$J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j<n} E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}}\otimes H_{\mathrm{out}}),$$
where the operator tensor is the tensor map of [[def-qc-tensor-map]] and the
tensor inner product is the finite product pairing in
[[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]].

The tensor factors are ordered input first and output second. The coordinate
matrix has size $(n\,\dim H_{\mathrm{out}})\times(n\,\dim H_{\mathrm{out}})$.
The chosen input basis is part of this definition. Empty input or output
bases give the corresponding empty sum and zero-dimensional Choi operator.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, fix an ordered
orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following four
conditions are equivalent:

1. $\Phi$ is a quantum channel.
2. $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)\succeq0$ and
   $\operatorname{Tr}_KJ_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)=I_H$.
3. $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^\dagger$ for a finite family of maps
$K_a:H\to K$ with
   $\sum_aK_a^\dagger K_a=I_H$.
4. There are a finite-dimensional $E$ and an isometry $V:H\to K\otimes E$
   with $\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger)$ for every $X$.

The Choi order is input factor first, output factor second.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

derivations.claim:
The matrix $Z$ is real and diagonal, so [F7] gives $Z^\dagger=Z$ and
$Z^2=I$ by direct multiplication [F8]. Thus
$K_0^\dagger K_0+K_1^\dagger K_1=pI+(1-p)I=I$, and [F5] makes $\Phi$
trace-preserving on all operators. By [F11], a density operator $\rho$ is
non-negative and has trace one. Self-adjointness gives the matrix form
$\rho=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\\overline b&d\end{pmatrix}$ with real $a,d$;
non-negativity applied to $e_0,e_1$ gives $a,d\ge0$, and trace one gives
$a+d=1$. Direct multiplication gives
$\Phi(\rho)=p\rho+(1-p)Z\rho Z=
\begin{pmatrix}a&(2p-1)b\\(2p-1)\overline b&d\end{pmatrix}$.
For every $x$, its quadratic form is
$\langle\Phi(\rho)x,x\rangle=
p\langle\rho x,x\rangle+(1-p)\langle\rho Zx,Zx\rangle\ge0$; the displayed
matrix is self-adjoint, and its trace is $a+d=1$. Thus the output is a
density operator. These formulas include $p=0$ and $p=1$.

Put $\lambda=2p-1$. Direct application of $Z$ to the four matrix units
gives $\Phi(E_{00})=E_{00}$, $\Phi(E_{11})=E_{11}$,
$\Phi(E_{01})=\lambda E_{01}$, and
$\Phi(E_{10})=\lambda E_{10}$. By [F3], in the ordered basis
$(e_0\otimes e_0,e_0\otimes e_1,e_1\otimes e_0,e_1\otimes e_1)$,
$$J(\Phi)=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&\lambda\\
0&0&0&0\\
0&0&0&0\\
\lambda&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.$$
The vectors $(e_0\otimes e_0\pm e_1\otimes e_1)/\sqrt2$ have eigenvalues
$1\pm\lambda=2p,2(1-p)$, and the other two product basis vectors have
eigenvalue zero. Since $p\in[0,1]$, every eigenvalue is nonnegative; the
matrix is self-adjoint, so [F6] makes $J(\Phi)$ non-negative.

In the product basis, the output partial-trace entry $(i,j)$ is
$\sum_{\alpha=0}^1J(\Phi)_{(i,\alpha),(j,\alpha)}$ by [F9]. The displayed
matrix in step 1.2 therefore gives diagonal entries $1,1$ and off-diagonal
entries $0,0$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_KJ(\Phi)=I_H$. The Choi positivity from
step 1.2 and this partial-trace identity imply by [F4] that $\Phi$ is a
channel; step 1.1 separately verifies the Kraus normalization and density
matrix action required in the Example.
